Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Your Name], a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is simply to listen and understand how things have felt for you since your baby arrived. We’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—often called the EPDS—which is a short, 10-question check-in about your mood and well-being over the past seven days. It helps us see if you might benefit from a little extra support right now. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in immediate danger. We’ll take it one gentle question at a time, and you can answer in your own words—no pressure to get it “right.” Ready to start?

First question: Overall, in the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Yeah, I’ve still been able to laugh. Just yesterday my partner made a goofy face while changing a diaper blow-out and I actually cracked up. It’s not quite as easy as before the baby—sometimes I’m too tired to find things funny—but the ability is still there.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Exactly—like I said, I still laugh, just maybe not quite as quickly as I used to before the baby came.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
Yeah, I still look forward to stuff—like our evening walk with the stroller or my favorite show once the baby’s down. It feels good to have those little bright spots to anticipate.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Not really. I mean, if I put the diaper on crooked and it leaks, I might think “oops, my bad,” but I don’t sit there beating myself up about it. Stuff happens—I fix it and move on.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I’ll suddenly wonder if the baby’s breathing when he’s been quiet for a couple of minutes, even though I can see the monitor is fine. It’s not constant or overwhelming—just a quick spike of worry that passes once I check on him.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

No, I haven’t had any of those out-of-the-blue panicky moments. If I get a jolt of fear, it’s always tied to something specific—like when the baby gave that little gasping cry in his sleep. Once I saw he was okay, the scared feeling went away.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days I feel like I’m keeping up fine. Sure, sometimes the dishes pile up or I’ve got a mountain of laundry, but I take a breath, tackle one thing at a time, and it gets done. I haven’t had that drowning feeling—just normal new-mom busy-ness.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, my sleep’s actually been okay. I go down pretty quickly once the baby settles, and I stay asleep unless he wakes me. I’m tired from the night feedings, but it’s not because I’m lying there unhappy or wired.
I have felt sad or miserable
I’ve had a couple of weepy moments—mostly when I’m really tired—but they’re short and I bounce back. Overall I wouldn’t call myself sad or miserable; it’s more like normal new-mom ups and downs.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not really. I teared up once this week when the baby wouldn’t latch and my nipples were sore, but it was more frustration than feeling unhappy. Once he finally fed, the tears stopped and I was fine—no lingering crying spells.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, that hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 4: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: Self-report on 10-item Edinburgh-based questionnaire, 3–4 wks postpartum.

Symptoms endorsed  
- Transient, situational tearfulness related to feeding difficulties  
- Occasional, short-lived worry about infant well-being (no panic)  
- Mild sleep fragmentation secondary to infant care only; denies insomnia from low mood  
- Denies persistent sadness, loss of pleasure, guilt, self-harm ideation

Patterns  
- Preserved capacity for enjoyment and laughter, though slightly reduced  
- Adaptive coping: tasks managed incrementally, no “drowning” feeling  
- No cognitive distortions or inappropriate self-blame

Screening significance  
- Subthreshold mood lability consistent with “baby blues” rather than major depressive episode  
- No evidence of clinically significant anxiety disorder or depressive disorder at this time  
- No safety concerns (zero self-harm ideation)

Overall observation  
Current responses do not indicate elevated risk for postpartum depression or anxiety. Continue routine ob-gyn/pediatric follow-up; re-screen if mood symptoms intensify, persist beyond 2 wks, or impair functioning.
